question_bank.stem: Why does the instructor motivate adversarial robustness at the start of the lecture?

options.text: AI systems are deployed broadly, creating more exposed attack surfaces.
AI datasets are shrinking quickly, creating fewer valid benchmarks.
AI hardware is changing rapidly, creating less stable optimization.
AI courses are adding visuals, creating more lecture examples.

question_bank.explanation: The stated motivation is deployment: more models in the wild means more systems that attackers can target.

distractor_rationales.B: Confuses deployment risk with benchmark availability.
distractor_rationales.C: Confuses security exposure with hardware changes.
distractor_rationales.D: Uses a lecture-format detail rather than the security motivation.

source_ref.evidence_span: because there are more and more AI models in the wild.

frame_evidence.description: Opening slide lists adversarial robustness and generative modeling while the instructor motivates deployment risk.

question_bank.stem: How does the lecture sequence the major technical topics after the opening motivation?

options.text: Generative models first, then adversarial defenses and prompt attacks.
Diffusion equations first, then GAN objectives and attack taxonomy.
Training backdoors first, then video generation and image captioning.
Adversarial robustness first, then generative modeling methods.

question_bank.explanation: The instructor explicitly says the first part covers adversarial robustness; the generative-modeling part comes later.

distractor_rationales.A: Reverses the order and narrows adversarial robustness to defenses.
distractor_rationales.B: Starts with a later diffusion topic and misorders GANs.
distractor_rationales.C: Mixes examples from different sections without matching the lecture order.

frame_evidence.description: Slide transition introduces the lecture plan with adversarial robustness before generative models.

question_bank.stem: In the early taxonomy, how are data poisoning attacks positioned relative to deployed models?

options.text: They alter outputs after training by planting data that later affects production behavior.
They alter outputs during inference by adding imperceptible pixel perturbations.
They alter outputs during prompting by hiding instructions inside user messages.
They alter outputs after decoding by filtering generated text from the model.

question_bank.explanation: Data poisoning is framed as an attacker influencing training data so the effect appears later when the model is in production.

distractor_rationales.B: Describes adversarial examples rather than poisoning.
distractor_rationales.C: Describes prompt injection rather than poisoned training data.
distractor_rationales.D: Describes an output-filtering defense rather than an attack vector.

source_ref.evidence_span: or data poisoning attacks, which is, as an attacker,

frame_evidence.description: Slide/class discussion groups attack waves, including data poisoning before prompt attacks.
